# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Consensus Trap

There is a quiet ritual that plays out in conference rooms every day. A discussion winds down, someone looks around the table and asks, "So are we all aligned?" Heads nod. Someone types up notes that say the group "agreed to move forward." The meeting ends on time, everyone feels productive, and the decision is recorded as settled.

Then, three weeks later, nothing has happened. Or worse: the project lurches in one direction while key people quietly pursue another, each convinced they were doing what the group wanted. When things fall apart, nobody can quite explain what went wrong. After all, everyone agreed.

The problem is that agreement is often an illusion. It can be genuine shared understanding, but it can also be politeness, fatigue, confusion, fear of the boss, or the simple human desire to get out of the room. A nod is not the same thing as conviction, and "sounds good to me" can mean anything from "I've thought this through and I'm with you" to "I have no idea what we just decided, but I don't want to look stupid by asking."
